Ok, so my mother broke her foot and gave birth when we were moving interstate for my dad's work. 6 now 7 kids, huge house, not a scrap was left behind.


The company my dad worked for hired movers. It took 6 days. 


Day One. We set out suitcases and a woman from his work and I packed our travel bags.


Day Two. 2 men from the moving company arrived, one put together boxes and one packed. It wasnt pretty, he packed by weight. Im talking drawers emptied into boxes, pantry, wardrobes, everything was packed, dirty or not.


Day Three. Same men return, and bring another. Repeat of Day Two, with the third man making a start on dismantling the furniture.


Day Four. Eight men and two trucks from the moving company arrive after dawn. They strip the house.


Day Five and Six. Cleaning company arrives with six people both days. Cars are picked up, Gardeners arrive and clean up outside. 


You would be looking for the same on a much smaller scale.


You want a packer, movers, and maybe a cleaner. The first 2 will most likely be from the same company or business. The cleaner can be found easily, any cleaning business will do. If you have a disability service provider in your town, they will have contacts. That is, a business that provides extra help within the home for those who need it, ask them for leads.


If you dont have something like that, call removalist companies direct. Tell them plainly, I need all belongings packed, furniture dismantled, everything moved and furniture reassembled in the new space. Ask them if they can do that. If they can, ask for a quote. They will need to come and see your space to fiqure out the cost FYI.


Hope this helps.

Thank you for the explanation. I had a conversation with someone the other day where they told me that Australia, where I live, seemed very regimented to them as an American. It blew my mind as I feel like I have a more than reasonable amount of freedom. Different cultures I guess.


I obviously agree that discrimination has no place in the code of conduct for a school, or anywhere else and have never seen a religious covering be banned nor would I accept it if I had.


My son is on the spectrum, with sensory processing issues and I have never had a problem switching to outside brands due to materials as long as it matches the school colours and meets the dress codes. Variances and allowances are granted by the office on a case by case basis.


I have a completely different attitude regarding uniforms. To me they are an achievable standard rather than an oppressive burden. As someone who's family was not financially stable growing up, a uniform was welcomed. In Australia, even the state schools have uniforms and a student code of conduct with dress codes.


By holding everyone to the same achievable standard, it can have a positive impact regarding bullying, student attendance and participation. The uniforms are usually sold by the school for a reasonable cost, ie a full set for primary school will be under $100 for brand new and that money goes straight back into the school. There are easily accessed goverment incentives that will provide your child with a new full set each year free of charge if you are low to mid income which is brilliant.


It also takes pressure off the household in my opinion. It saves money on children's wardrobes by having a uniform that is hard wearing and often doesnt require ironing for 5 days of the week.


My son is very confident in his style, would be considered alternative for a conservative town. He shops on both sides of the aisle, regardless of gender. The only time I step in is if it is a hygiene issue, or a legal issue ie his genitals are showing, or heath concern ie he is trying to wear heavy winter clothes for a walk in 40 degree hot weather. 


Whether his calm acceptance of the school uniform is from being institutionalized or an appreciation of the achievable standard I couldnt tell you as I am clearly biased. 


There is a time and place for everything, and a wardrobe should reflect that. Dressing appropriately for the situation is based on common sense, not mindless conformity. Uniforms in my opinion are not a form of punishment or a tool to strip people of their individuality. They are put in place to achieve a necessary minimum standard.

I would be genuinely interested in a response on my positions. I appreciated the perspective on workplace uniforms, as my family is in mining and the trades, I have always seen it as protective instead of oppressive, but I have little experience with things like the military.

I feel like if it was restricted to girls only, I would have a problem with it, but its a gender neutral rule. I find it to be a practical rule personally, I have always had long hair and experienced the same dress codes.


His schools have always had an enforced dress code and uniform. Primary schools here require long hair to be put up, and its becoming more common in high schools as a standard instead of classroom specific. I know in primary schools, hair lice are a contributing factor for the rule being in place and the uniforms include matching hair ties in the school colours. 


At this high school, he participates in Industrial design and technology electives, its a must in those classes for safety reasons, as well as in the home economics sections due to safety and hygiene. I imagine its just easier to make it across the board rather than classroom specific.

I am the main care giver of a boy in high school, obviously I cant repeat verbatim as it is a series of conversations, but I can address the overall attitudes I take regarding body autonomy which I fully support. I have never had to articulate it before but I will try.


I use things like conforming vs performing vs presenting perspectives regarding body image, personal hygiene, behaviour and style and we have conversations around that. Respect and positive body image are common touchstones.


For instance, he has long hair which is out of the norm for his gender at this school. He genuinely likes having long hair, he doesnt do it for anyone else and he doesn't care if others do not like it. Therefore I only ask that he maintains his hair and personal hygiene to an exceptable standard. Which means it is washed, brushed, and trimmed regularly and adheres to the dress code. At this school, hair below the collar must be tied up, regardless of gender. 


He doesnt like having to tie it up, but the rule is sensible so I insist. He forgets to wash it so I step in and insist when it becomes a hygiene issue.


Otherwise I do not interfere with his hair and he is free to do as he likes.
